episodes.title: Episode 02: How it sees, decides and clicks
notes: One prompt per loop pass: screenshot until still, read the prompt line, run its handler
Hand names are fuzzy-matched (>= 80% similar) to this game's cards; counters give actions, coins, buys
Buys come from dominion-v1's own play_buy_phase on a stand-in state (buy targets + terminal density included)
Clicks: glide, rest 0.35 s, press and hold 0.15 s, via XTEST
Memory per game in autopilot/run_<seed>.json; rematch with --games N
transcript: This episode goes through the autopilot one part at a time, in the order it works during a turn. If you want to see it, the film called How it works shows the same steps on recorded footage.
Everything runs in one loop. Each pass handles exactly one thing the game asks for. And each pass has three parts. The eyes, the brain, and the hands.

The eyes start with a screenshot of the game window. Before it reads anything, the autopilot takes a second screenshot a third of a second later. It compares the two. If they differ, the game is still moving, so it waits and tries again. Only a still screen gets read.

Then it reads the prompt line. That is the sentence just under the supply. It says things like play action cards, play treasure cards, or buy a card. The prompt decides which handler runs next. A prompt it doesn't recognise is saved as a picture, and the autopilot waits for you.

If the prompt asks for actions, it reads the hand. Every card has its name on a banner at the top, and the text reader returns each name with its position. Those positions are where it will click later. The names are matched against the cards in this game. A small reading mistake, like State instead of Estate, still matches, as long as the two are eighty percent alike or more.

Next it reads the counters. They are three small numbers left of the hand, for actions, coins and buys. In the action phase it waits until the actions counter shows at least one, because a zero means the turn is still starting.

Now the brain. The evolved strategy splits the game into three phases. In this model the early phase is just the first two turns. The middle lasts until only two provinces are left, or until turn sixteen. After that comes the late phase. Each phase has its own buy list. Early, it wants Smithy above everything. In the middle, Province, then Gold, then Silver. Late, Province, then Duchy.

For actions it keeps two lists. Cards that give back an action, like Merchant or Market, are played first. Then the terminal cards, like Smithy. It skips a Moneylender when there is no Copper in hand to trash.

Buying is the part I am most careful about. The autopilot doesn't re-write the buy rules. It builds a stand-in game state. That state holds the coins and buys it just read, the cards it owns, and a supply without the cards the strategy never learned. Then it calls the buy function from the original training engine, and uses whatever that function buys. This brings along two rules that are easy to forget. One caps how many copies of a card to own. The other refuses a terminal action card when the deck has no spare actions to play it.

The hands come last. Clicks are sent through an X eleven extension called X test. The game only accepts a click after a short hover. So the pointer glides in, rests for about a third of a second, and then presses and holds. Hand cards are clicked a little below their name, on the card itself, because a hovered card lifts up.

Between turns, the autopilot keeps a small memory file named after the game's seed. It holds the turn number, the provinces left, the cards it owns, and any piles it found empty. If you stop it in the middle of a game and start it again, it reads that file and carries on.

At the end, the score screen appears. The autopilot reads the points, saves a picture of the screen, and stops. Or, if you asked for more games, it presses rematch and starts again with the new kingdom.
That is the whole machine. In the next episode, I'll tell you what the recorded games revealed, and how you can run it yourself.

episodes.title: Episode 01: From a simulator to the Steam game
notes: The evolved strategy (dominion-v1) beats Big Money 73% and its hall of fame 54% in its own engine
Steam Dominion runs under Proton as an XWayland window: screenshots (~50 ms) and XTEST clicks work without a permission prompt
The kingdom comes from the game's own save file (gamelocal_*.xml)
Clicks only register after a hover; clicks during animations are lost
First full game: won 58-8 against Very Easy AI in 21 turns
transcript: You asked a simple question. Could the Dominion strategy from your genetic algorithm project play the real Dominion game on Steam? This episode is the story of how it got there, and what was in the way.

The strategy comes from a project that evolved Dominion players inside its own small game engine. It played thousands of games, kept the winners, and mixed and mutated them. What came out is one small file of lists. What to buy early, in the middle, and late. Which action cards to play first. What to trash with a Chapel. In its own engine it beats the simple Big Money strategy about three games in four, and it wins just over half its games against its own hall of fame.

The Steam game is a different world. It is a closed Windows program that runs on Linux through Proton. There is no way for a bot to plug in. No interface, no mods, and no file that lists the cards in your hand. So the only way in was the way a person plays. Look at the screen, decide, and click.

The first worry was the desktop. Your machine runs Wayland, and Wayland is built to stop one program from watching another. But Proton runs the game as an old style X eleven window, inside a layer called X Wayland. Inside that layer, a program can still copy a window's pixels. The first screenshot came back in about a twentieth of a second, with no permission dialog. A test click on the play treasures button worked too. That was the moment the project became possible.

The second piece was knowing the kingdom. Here the game helped. It saves each local game as a small text file, and one line of it lists the ten kingdom cards. So the autopilot never has to recognise the supply. It reads the list, then finds each pile on screen by its name.

Reading the screen is done by a text recognition model called Rapid O C R. It runs on the processor, on a few small regions. The prompt line says what the game wants. The hand shows the cards. And three counters show actions, coins and buys.

Then came the first surprise. The click on the Silver pile did nothing. It turned out the game only accepts a click after the pointer has hovered over the target for a moment. So every click now glides in, rests for about a third of a second, and then presses. After that, buying worked.

The second surprise was timing. At the start of a turn, the game animates, and clicks made during that animation are lost. Smithy sometimes needed three clicks. The fix was to wait for a still screen, and to wait until the actions counter shows at least one.

For the decisions, the autopilot doesn't copy the strategy's rules. It builds a stand-in game state from what it read, and calls the original buy function from the training engine. So the purchases on Steam are exactly the purchases the evolved strategy makes in training.

The first full game was against the very easy computer opponent. The autopilot bought Silver, Smithy, three Golds, and then Province after Province. It won fifty eight to eight, in twenty one turns, without any help.

That is where the first episode ends. The next one goes through every part in detail. The one after that is about what the recorded games revealed, including two bugs that only showed up in real play.
